# Role Models (2008)

*   Post author By [Dan Stalcup](https://thegoodsreviews.com/author/dan/)
*   Post date11/14/2022
*   No Comments on Role Models (2008)

![Image 2](https://thegoodsreviews.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/u2L2pRaJjMbpEXdqlxHv0jf6vT1-1200x675.jpg)

Many comedians and filmmakers got a boost during the Judd Apatow surge of the late 2000s. For example, David Wain, the subversive filmmaker known for the cult comedy Wet Hot American Summer, rode the wave to release his most conventional and popular comedy, the distinctly Apatovian but non-Apatow-produced picture Role Models.

Role Models is notable for giving platform to a whole bunch of talented comedians who would go on to be the comedy equivalent of character actors (I guess still just called “character actors”) — funny people who are liable to show up in any film or TV show in an unexpected role, almost always improving what they appear in. A few of the people here even got major roles at some point. So many of these faces became “where did I see them before?” actors for the next few years, and ultimately beloved presences: Jane Lynch, Ken Jeong, Joe Lo Truglio, Ken Marino, Matt Walsh, Louis CK, Keegan-Michael Key, Kerri Kenney, etc. And that discounts the cast members I already knew and loved: Paul Rudd, Elizabeth Banks, Seann William Scott, Christopher “McLovin” Mintz-Plasse.

![Image 3](https://thegoodsreviews.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/vDKbYwjtQ5XMWIEmlnoMi5kaqYm-1024x576.jpg)

Role Models follows Wheeler (Scott) and Danny (Rudd), energy drink salesmen who go from school to school hawking the product in the guise of an anti-drug PSA. One day, Danny faces an existential crisis and goes on a bender which results in his and Wheeler’s arrest. Their penalty: they must volunteer in a Big Brothers/Big Sisters type mentorship program as community service. They must become… role models.

The problem with the story is that both Wheeler and Danny are colossal assholes at the start of the film. I did not care if bad things happened to them. This is in contrast with most of the man-child comedies of the era that went out of their way to make their flawed protagonists endearing. Wheeler and Danny’s shittiness was a big turn-off for me when the movie first debuted; I like laughing at AND rooting for my heroes. These days, I’m here a little bit less for the storytelling, and frankly don’t mind that it has a bit of nastiness to it. But be warned that these are not especially likable heroes.

![Image 4](https://thegoodsreviews.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/zqwwX2sHnNS9lZGIDZ7HC7E8EPB-1024x576.jpg)

Wheeler and Danny get assigned polar opposite kids to mentor: Wheeler, a party bro, is paired with with profane tween Ronnie (Bobb’e J. Thompson). Meanwhile, the neurotic Danny is paired with Augie (Mintz-Plasse), a dorky LARPer whose parents hate him. It creates a fun web of odd couple dynamic between the various leads, with solid cast chemistry all around. (One hiccup: It is odd and slightly problematic that the main black character is a crude, gangsta-rap inspired wild-child, but I’m inclined to give the movie the benefit of the doubt.)

The movie really picks up in the third act when the leads enter a large-scale LARP’ing battle, which pulls all of the film’s ensemble into one big set piece. Role Models is a funny movie, funnier than I remembered to be honest, and holds together just well enough from a story perspective by the end, but doesn’t have quite enough show-stoppers or lines you’ll be quoting for years like the best of its kin. # Role Models (2008)

*   Post author By [Dan Stalcup](https://thegoodsreviews.com/author/dan/)
*   Post date11/14/2022
*   No Comments on Role Models (2008)

![Image 2](https://thegoodsreviews.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/u2L2pRaJjMbpEXdqlxHv0jf6vT1-1200x675.jpg)

Many comedians and filmmakers got a boost during the Judd Apatow surge of the late 2000s. For example, David Wain, the subversive filmmaker known for the cult comedy Wet Hot American Summer, rode the wave to release his most conventional and popular comedy, the distinctly Apatovian but non-Apatow-produced picture Role Models.

Role Models is notable for giving platform to a whole bunch of talented comedians who would go on to be the comedy equivalent of character actors (I guess still just called “character actors”) — funny people who are liable to show up in any film or TV show in an unexpected role, almost always improving what they appear in. A few of the people here even got major roles at some point. So many of these faces became “where did I see them before?” actors for the next few years, and ultimately beloved presences: Jane Lynch, Ken Jeong, Joe Lo Truglio, Ken Marino, Matt Walsh, Louis CK, Keegan-Michael Key, Kerri Kenney, etc. And that discounts the cast members I already knew and loved: Paul Rudd, Elizabeth Banks, Seann William Scott, Christopher “McLovin” Mintz-Plasse.

![Image 3](https://thegoodsreviews.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/vDKbYwjtQ5XMWIEmlnoMi5kaqYm-1024x576.jpg)

Role Models follows Wheeler (Scott) and Danny (Rudd), energy drink salesmen who go from school to school hawking the product in the guise of an anti-drug PSA. One day, Danny faces an existential crisis and goes on a bender which results in his and Wheeler’s arrest. Their penalty: they must volunteer in a Big Brothers/Big Sisters type mentorship program as community service. They must become… role models.

The problem with the story is that both Wheeler and Danny are colossal assholes at the start of the film. I did not care if bad things happened to them. This is in contrast with most of the man-child comedies of the era that went out of their way to make their flawed protagonists endearing. Wheeler and Danny’s shittiness was a big turn-off for me when the movie first debuted; I like laughing at AND rooting for my heroes. These days, I’m here a little bit less for the storytelling, and frankly don’t mind that it has a bit of nastiness to it. But be warned that these are not especially likable heroes.

![Image 4](https://thegoodsreviews.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/zqwwX2sHnNS9lZGIDZ7HC7E8EPB-1024x576.jpg)

Wheeler and Danny get assigned polar opposite kids to mentor: Wheeler, a party bro, is paired with with profane tween Ronnie (Bobb’e J. Thompson). Meanwhile, the neurotic Danny is paired with Augie (Mintz-Plasse), a dorky LARPer whose parents hate him. It creates a fun web of odd couple dynamic between the various leads, with solid cast chemistry all around. (One hiccup: It is odd and slightly problematic that the main black character is a crude, gangsta-rap inspired wild-child, but I’m inclined to give the movie the benefit of the doubt.)

The movie really picks up in the third act when the leads enter a large-scale LARP’ing battle, which pulls all of the film’s ensemble into one big set piece. It also pays off on the movie’s best emotional thread: Danny teaching Augie to stand up for what makes him happy rather than what his parents want.

Of the many supporting turns, Lynch is terrific, but Lo Truglio is the real scene stealer, leaning into dramatic Tolkien-esque diction and enunciation for some hilarious delivery. It honestly might be the best he’s ever been used in a movie I’ve watched.

Role Models is a funny movie, funnier than I remembered to be honest, and holds together just well enough from a story perspective by the end, but doesn’t have quite enough show-stoppers or lines you’ll be quoting for years like the best of its kin. (E.g, there’s a running joke about Starbucks’ weird names for things that’s low-hanging fruit. Yeah, “venti” is kind of dumb, but literally every person who’s bought a coffee has made these jokes.) Nonetheless, I’m glad I caught up with Role Models. I laughed a lot and was reminded how much I enjoy spending time with this cast.

_**The Artist**_ is a 2011 French-Belgian[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-the_artist_2011-2)[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-9)[comedy-drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy-drama "Comedy-drama") film[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-11) in the style of a [black-and-white](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black-and-white "Black-and-white")[silent film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film") or [part-talkie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Part-talkie "Part-talkie").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-ACEFilmEditors-12)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-RottenTomatoes-14)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-15) It was written and directed by [Michel Hazanavicius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Hazanavicius "Michel Hazanavicius"), produced by [Thomas Langmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Langmann "Thomas Langmann") and stars [Jean Dujardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Dujardin "Jean Dujardin") and [Bérénice Bejo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo "Bérénice Bejo").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-16) The story takes place in [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los Angeles"), between 1927 and 1932, and focuses on the relationship between a rising young actress and an older silent film star as silent cinema falls out of fashion and is replaced by the "[talkies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_film "Sound film")".

_The Artist_ received widespread critical acclaim and won many accolades. Dujardin won [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival_Award_for_Best_Actor "Cannes Film Festival Award for Best Actor") at the [2011 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Cannes_Film_Festival "2011 Cannes Film Festival"), where the film premiered. The film was nominated for six [Golden Globes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award "Golden Globe Award"), the most of any 2011 film, and won three: [Best Motion Picture– Musical or Comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Motion_Picture_%E2%80%93_Musical_or_Comedy "Golden Globe Award for Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy"), [Best Original Score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Original_Score "Golden Globe Award for Best Original Score"), and [Best Actor– Motion Picture Musical or Comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Actor_%E2%80%93_Motion_Picture_Musical_or_Comedy "Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Motion Picture Musical or Comedy") for Dujardin. In January 2012, it was nominated for twelve [BAFTAs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA "BAFTA"), the most of any film from 2011,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-BBCBAFTA-17) and won seven, including [Best Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Film "BAFTA Award for Best Film"), [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Direction "BAFTA Award for Best Direction"), [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Actor_in_a_Leading_Role "BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role") for Dujardin, and [Best Original Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay "BAFTA Award for Best Original Screenplay") for Hazanavicius.

It was nominated for ten [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") and won five,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-BBCOscar-18) including [Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture"), [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director") for Hazanavicius, and [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor "Academy Award for Best Actor") for Dujardin, making him the first French actor ever to win in this category. It was also the first non-American/non-British film to ever win Best Picture,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-19) the first mainly silent film to win since 1927's _[Wings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wings\_(1927\_film) "Wings (1927 film)")_ won at the [1st Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Academy_Awards "1st Academy Awards") in 1929, the first film presented in the [4:3 aspect ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspect_ratio "Aspect ratio") to win since 1953's _[From Here to Eternity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/From\_Here\_to\_Eternity "From Here to Eternity")_, the first [black-and-white film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black-and-white_movie "Black-and-white movie") to win since 1993's _[Schindler's List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schindler's\_List "Schindler's List")_, though the latter contained limited colour sequences; and the first 100% black-and-white film to win since 1960's _[The Apartment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Apartment "The Apartment")_.

In France it was nominated for ten [César Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar_Awards "César Awards"),[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-BBCCesar-20) winning six, including [Best Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar_Award_for_Best_Film "César Award for Best Film"), [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar_Award_for_Best_Director "César Award for Best Director") for Hazanavicius, and [Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar_Award_for_Best_Actress "César Award for Best Actress") for Bejo. _The Artist_ has received more awards than any other French film.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-21)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

In 1927, [silent film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film") star George Valentin is posing for pictures outside the [premiere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiere "Premiere") of his latest hit film when a young woman, Peppy Miller, accidentally bumps into him. Valentin reacts with humor and shows off with Peppy for the cameras. The next day, Peppy is on the front page of _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ with the headline "Who's That Girl?" She capitalizes by auditioning as a dancer and is spotted by Valentin, who insists that she have a part in Kinograph Studios' next production, despite objections from studio boss Al Zimmer. While performing a scene in which they dance together, Valentin and Peppy show great chemistry. With a little guidance from Valentin, who draws a [beauty spot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_spot "Beauty spot") on her cheek, Peppy rises through the industry, earning more prominent starring roles.

Two years later, Zimmer announces plans to cease production of silent films at Kinograph Studios, but Valentin is dismissive, insisting that sound is just a fad. In a dream, he begins hearing sounds from his environment (as does the audience) but cannot speak himself. He decides to leave the studio for the chance to produce, finance, and direct his own silent film, _Tears of Love_. The film opens on the same day as Peppy's new sound film _Beauty Spot_ and the [1929 stock market crash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_crash_of_1929 "Wall Street crash of 1929"). Valentin's only chance of avoiding bankruptcy is for his film to be a hit. Unfortunately, audiences flock to Peppy's film instead, while only a few people attend Valentin's. With Valentin ruined, his wife, Doris, kicks him out, and he moves into an apartment with his valet/chauffeur, Clifton, and his dog. Peppy quickly becomes the first of several major new Hollywood sound film stars.

Later, the bankrupt Valentin is forced to auction his personal effects, and after realizing he has not paid the loyal Clifton in over a year, gives him his car before firing him. Depressed and drunk, Valentin sets fire to a stack of his old films. As the [nitrate film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrocellulose#Film "Nitrocellulose") blazes out of control, he is overwhelmed by the smoke and passes out inside the burning house, clutching a single film canister. However, Valentin's dog attracts the help of a nearby policeman, and after being rescued, Valentin is hospitalized for injuries suffered in the fire. Peppy visits the hospital and discovers that the film he rescued is the one with them dancing together. She asks for him to be moved to her house to recuperate. Valentin awakens in a bed at her house to find that Clifton is now working for Peppy. His ego hurt, Valentin shows ingratitude for Peppy having taken him in, prompting Clifton to remind him of his changing luck.

Peppy insists to Zimmer that Valentin co-star in her next film, threatening to quit Kinograph if he does not agree. After Valentin learns that Peppy bought his possessions at auction, he returns in despair to his burnt-out apartment. Peppy arrives and finds that Valentin is about to attempt suicide. She tells him she only wanted to help him. They embrace, and Valentin tells her it is no use; no one wants to hear him speak. Remembering Valentin's superb dancing ability, Peppy persuades Zimmer to let her make a [musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_film#The_classical_sound_era "Musical film") production so Valentin can avoid the humiliation of having to speak.

Now the audience hears sound for the second time, as the film starts rolling for a dance scene with Peppy and Valentin and their tap-dancing can be heard. Once the choreography is complete, the two dancers are heard panting. The director of the musical calls, "Cut!" to which Zimmer adds: "Perfect. Beautiful. Could you give me just one more?" Valentin, in his only audible line, replies "With pleasure," revealing a [French accent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_accent "French accent").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-themarysue-22) The camera then pulls back to the sounds of the film crew as they prepare to shoot another take.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")]

### Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/%C3%89quipe_The_Artist_Cannes_2011.jpg/500px-%C3%89quipe_The_Artist_Cannes_2011.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%C3%89quipe_The_Artist_Cannes_2011.jpg)

Some of the cast and crew at the [2011 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Cannes_Film_Festival "2011 Cannes Film Festival"): (left to right), score composer [Ludovic Bource](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludovic_Bource "Ludovic Bource"), director [Michel Hazanavicius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Hazanavicius "Michel Hazanavicius"), stars [Missi Pyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missi_Pyle "Missi Pyle"), [Bérénice Bejo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo "Bérénice Bejo"), and [Jean Dujardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Dujardin "Jean Dujardin"), director of photography [Guillaume Schiffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_Schiffman "Guillaume Schiffman") and producer [Thomas Langmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Langmann "Thomas Langmann").

Director [Michel Hazanavicius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Hazanavicius "Michel Hazanavicius") had been fantasizing about making a [silent film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film") for many years, both because many filmmakers he admires emerged in the silent era, and because of the image-driven nature of the form. According to Hazanavicius, his wish to make a silent film was at first not taken seriously, but after the financial success of his spy-film pastiches _[OSS 117: Cairo, Nest of Spies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OSS\_117:\_Cairo,\_Nest\_of\_Spies "OSS 117: Cairo, Nest of Spies")_ and _[OSS 117: Lost in Rio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OSS\_117:\_Lost\_in\_Rio "OSS 117: Lost in Rio")_, producers started to express interest. The forming of the film's narrative started with Hazanavicius' desire to work again with actors [Jean Dujardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Dujardin "Jean Dujardin") and [Bérénice Bejo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo "Bérénice Bejo"), who had both starred in _OSS 117: Cairo, Nest of Spies_. Hazanavicius chose the form of a [melodrama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melodrama_(film_genre) "Melodrama (film genre)"), mostly because he thought many of the films from the silent era that have aged best are of that genre. He did extensive research about 1920s Hollywood, and studied silent films to find the right techniques to make the story comprehensible without having to use too many [intertitles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertitle "Intertitle"). The screenplay took four months to write and was principally inspired by the 1928 silent comedy, _[Show People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Show\_People "Show People")_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-presskitmh-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-24)

Chief among the influences shaping the screenplay's protagonist was [Douglas Fairbanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Fairbanks "Douglas Fairbanks"). The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences' recent book _Douglas Fairbanks_, by [Jeffrey Vance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Vance "Jeffrey Vance"), as well as the academy's Douglas Fairbanks exhibition and screening events both in Los Angeles and New York City, afforded Hollywood's first swashbuckling hero and the academy's first president some significant media attention.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-25)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-26)

### Filming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Filming")]

[Principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") on _The Artist_ began in November 2010,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-27) taking place over the course of thirty-five days,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-BAFTARed-28) made in the 1.33:1 screen ratio commonly used in the silent film era. Though presented in black-and-white, it was shot in color by [cinematographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinematographer "Cinematographer")[Guillaume Schiffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_Schiffman "Guillaume Schiffman").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-time-29) All the technical details, including lenses, lighting and camera moves, were calibrated to aesthetically match silent films of the period.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-30) To recreate the slightly sped-up look of 1920s silent films, the film was shot at a slightly lower [frame rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frame_rate "Frame rate") of 22 fps as opposed to the standard 24 fps.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-31) Most of the film is silent, except for two brief scenes with sound as well as the [non-diegetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinematic_techniques#Sound "Cinematic techniques") soundtrack. Throughout the shoot, Hazanavicius played music from classic Hollywood films while the actors performed.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-presskitmh-23)

The film was produced by La Petite Reine and ARP Sélection for 13.47 million euro, including co-production support from [Studio 37](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_37 "Studio 37") and [France 3 Cinéma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_3_Cin%C3%A9ma "France 3 Cinéma"), and pre-sales investment from [StudioCanal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/StudioCanal "StudioCanal") and CinéCinéma.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-outofcomp-32) The cast and the crew included both French and American members.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-presskitmh-23) All the scenes were shot in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), primarily in [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los Angeles"), but also in downtown theaters, restaurants and houses, including the one in which [Mary Pickford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Pickford "Mary Pickford") lived. Soundstage work was done at [Red Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren-Mar_Studios "Ren-Mar Studios"), and the studio lot itself doubled for part of the fictional Kinograph Studios lot, with Red's Lillian Way entrance doubling as the Kinograph entrance in several sequences. The iconic [Bradbury Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradbury_Building "Bradbury Building") in downtown L.A. provided the location for the film's distinctive staircase sequence. The dance sequence that closes the film took seventeen takes, and required Dujardin and Bejo to spend five months studying tap dancing, with Dujardin claiming that "in the first week it's fun, the fifth week it's a little boring, at the end it's thrilling".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-33)

American [costume designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costume_design "Costume design")[Mark Bridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Bridges_(costume_designer) "Mark Bridges (costume designer)") created the wardrobe for the film's cast.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-sfgate-34)

### Music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Music")]

Main article: [_The Artist_ (soundtrack)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(soundtrack) "The Artist (soundtrack)")

The [film's music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_score "Film score") was largely composed by [Ludovic Bource](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludovic_Bource "Ludovic Bource"), but includes works by other composers such as [Alberto Ginastera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Ginastera "Alberto Ginastera")'s "Estancia". The soundtrack was recorded in Belgium by the [Brussels Philharmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels_Philharmonic "Brussels Philharmonic") and was conducted by Ernst Van Tiel; the Brussels Jazz Orchestra also cooperated. The recording took place during six days in April 2011 at [Flagey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_Flagey "Place Flagey")'s Studio 4 in Brussels.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-35)

The film's climactic scene is set to [Bernard Herrmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Herrmann "Bernard Herrmann")'s "Scène d'amour" from [his score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertigo_(film_score) "Vertigo (film score)") to [Alfred Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock "Alfred Hitchcock")'s film _[Vertigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertigo\_(film) "Vertigo (film)")_. In _Vertigo_, that composition similarly accompanies an extended scene without dialogue. Only one song (sung, with lyrics) is used in the soundtrack, "[Pennies from Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennies_from_Heaven_(song) "Pennies from Heaven (song)")", sung by [Rose "Chi-Chi" Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_Murphy "Rose Murphy") (uncredited). This song was written in 1936 although the film is set between 1927 and 1932. The soundtrack was released on 10 October in France, and 21 October in the U.K. and U.S. through [Sony Classical Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Classical_Records "Sony Classical Records").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-36)

The film premiered on 15 May 2011 in competition at the [2011 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Cannes_Film_Festival "2011 Cannes Film Festival").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Cannes-37) It was initially announced as an out of competition entry, but was moved to the competition a week before the festival opened.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-38) The French regular release was on 12 October 2011 through [Warner Bros. France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros.").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-39)[The Weinstein Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Weinstein_Company "The Weinstein Company") bought the distribution rights for the US, UK, Australia, South Africa, Latin America and Eastern Europe, with the film also selling to Comstock and GAGA in Japan and Delphi Film in Germany.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-40) The film was initially given a [limited release](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited_release "Limited release") in the United States on 23 November 2011.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-41)

Following its wins at the [69th Golden Globe Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/69th_Golden_Globe_Awards "69th Golden Globe Awards"), it was announced Warner Bros. would re-release the film in France in 362 theaters on 25 January 2012.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-42)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-43) It was also re-released in Belgium on 22 February 2012.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-44)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Box office

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Box office")]

_The Artist_ grossed $44,671,682 in North America, along with $88,761,174 in other territories for a worldwide total of $133,432,856.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Boxofficemojo-3) After its success at the Academy Awards, the film saw a moderate boost the following week on the box office in North America. It appeared on the week's top 10 chart and got an increase of 34% while expanding its release from 966 theaters to 1,756.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-47)

### Critical response

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Critical response")]

On review aggregator [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes") the film has an approval rating of 95% based on 327 reviews, with an average rating of 8.8/10. The website's critical consensus states, "A crowd-pleasing tribute to the magic of silent cinema, _The Artist_ is a clever, joyous film with delightful performances and visual style to spare."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-RottenTomatoes-14) At [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which assigns a [weighted average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_average "Weighted average") rating to reviews, the film received an average score of 89 out of 100, based on 41 critics, indicating "universal acclaim".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Metacritic-48) Audiences surveyed by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film an average grade of "A" on an A+ to F scale.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-49)

Mark Adams of _[Screen Daily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen\_International "Screen International")_ called the film "a real pleasure"; "propelled elegantly forward by delightful performances from Jean Dujardin and Bérénice Bejo it is the most unlikely of feel-good movies." He added however: "The film does feel a little sluggish towards the end of the first third as the music is a little repetitive and the intertitles are infrequent, but Hazanavicius manages to give the film a real sense of charm and warmth, and film fans will be competing to spot visual and musical references."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-50) Peter Bradshaw of _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ described how the film "had me on my feet cheering throughout the final credits" and stated "I can't wait to see it again".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-51)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Jean_Dujardin_2014.jpg/250px-Jean_Dujardin_2014.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jean_Dujardin_2014.jpg)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo_2014_2.jpg/250px-B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo_2014_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo_2014_2.jpg)

The performances of [Jean Dujardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Dujardin "Jean Dujardin") and [Bérénice Bejo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo "Bérénice Bejo") garnered critical acclaim, earning them [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") nominations for [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor "Academy Award for Best Actor") and [Best Supporting Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress") respectively, with Dujardin winning his category.

Geoffrey McNab at _[The Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Independent "The Independent")_ called the film "both a surefire crowdpleaser and a magnificent piece of film-making" in his 5 star review from the [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-52) Rick Groen of _[The Globe and Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Globe\_and\_Mail "The Globe and Mail")_ assessed _The Artist_ highly, noting the film "uses old technology to dazzling effect to illustrate the insistent conquest of a new technology."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-53) Sukanya Verma for [Rediff.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rediff.com "Rediff.com") feels _The Artist_ is an extremely well-researched film and is an instant classic.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Review_:_The_Artist-54) David Thomson of _[The New Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Republic "The New Republic")_ called _The Artist_ an "accomplished and witty entertainment" and went on to write, "Whether Hazanavicius can do more things as elegant and touching, without the gimmick of silence, remains to be seen (and heard). Meanwhile, he is to be congratulated on the grounds of pleasure alone. He may be due for much more in the way of rewards."[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-55)_[Chicago Sun-Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago\_Sun-Times "Chicago Sun-Times")_[film critic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_criticism "Film criticism")[Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") gave the film four out of four stars, praising the performances, and calling the film "one of the most entertaining films in many a moon, a film that charms because of its story, its performances and because of the sly way it plays with being silent and black and white."[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-56)

Writing for _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant\_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_, Jaime N. Christley gave the film one-and-a-half out of four stars, explaining Michel Hazanavicius ignores "everything that's fascinating and memorable about the era, focusing instead on a patchwork of general knowledge, so eroded of inconvenient facts that it doesn't even qualify as a _roman à clef_."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-57)_[America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America\_(magazine) "America (magazine)")_ argued that while Jean Dujardin carried the film, Bejo's performance was disappointing.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-america-58)

### Kim Novak controversy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Kim Novak controversy")]

On 9 January 2012, actress [Kim Novak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Novak "Kim Novak") stated that "rape" had been metaphorically committed in the film's licensed use of a portion of [Bernard Herrmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Herrmann "Bernard Herrmann")'s score from [Alfred Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock "Alfred Hitchcock")'s 1958 film _[Vertigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertigo\_(film) "Vertigo (film)")_ (in which Novak starred). The final portion of _The Artist_ is accompanied not by original music, but by a 1992 recording of the Herrmann composition _Scene d'Amour_, conducted by [Elmer Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elmer_Bernstein "Elmer Bernstein"). In the article published, by _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_, she stated that "I feel as if my body—or at least my body of work—has been violated by the movie."[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Vertigo-59) "This film should've been able to stand on its own without depending on Bernard Herrmann's score from Alfred Hitchcock's _Vertigo_ to provide more drama" and that "It is morally wrong for the artistry of our industry to use and abuse famous pieces of work to gain attention and applause for other than what they were intended", ending her comments with "Shame on them!"[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-CNN-60)

In response, director Hazanavicius released a statement:

> _The Artist_ was made as a love letter to cinema, and grew out of my (and all of my cast and crew's) admiration and respect for movies throughout history. It was inspired by the work of Hitchcock, [Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Lang "Fritz Lang"), [Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ford "John Ford"), [Lubitsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Lubitsch "Ernst Lubitsch"), [Murnau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._W._Murnau "F. W. Murnau") and [Wilder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Wilder "Billy Wilder"). I love Bernard Herrmann and his music has been used in many different films and I'm very pleased to have it in mine. I respect Kim Novak greatly and I'm sorry to hear she disagrees.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-61)

Hazanavicius also told [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN") "I used music from another movie, but it's not illegal. We paid for that, we asked for that and we had the permission to do it. For me there is no real controversy.... I feel sorry for her, but there's a lot of movies with music from other movies, directors do that all the time and I'm not sure it's a big deal."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-CNN-60)

In May 2011, when the film was first shown at the Cannes Festival, [Todd McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todd_McCarthy "Todd McCarthy") from _[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hollywood\_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")_ mentioned the use of Herrmann's music, "Hazanavicius and Bource daringly choose to explicitly employ Bernard Herrmann's love theme from _Vertigo_, which is dramatically effective in its own right but is so well known that it yanks you out of one film and places you in the mind-set of another. Surely some sort of reworked equivalent would have been a better idea."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-McCarthy-62)

### Accolades

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Accolades")]

Main article: [List of accolades received by _The Artist_ (film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_accolades_received_by_The_Artist_(film) "List of accolades received by The Artist (film)")

At the [65th British Academy Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_British_Academy_Film_Awards "65th British Academy Film Awards"), the film won seven awards, including Best Film, Best Actor for Dujardin, Best Original Screenplay for Hazanavicius, Cinematography for Schiffman, Costume Design for Bridges and Original Score for [Ludovic Bource](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludovic_Bource "Ludovic Bource").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Orange_BAFTA_Film_Award_Winners-63)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-BAFTA_2012_Winners-64) At the [69th Golden Globe Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/69th_Golden_Globe_Awards "69th Golden Globe Awards"), the film was nominated for six [Golden Globes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globes "Golden Globes") to win three of them; [Best Motion Picture– Musical or Comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Motion_Picture_%E2%80%93_Musical_or_Comedy "Golden Globe Award for Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy"), [Best Actor– Motion Picture Musical or Comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Actor_%E2%80%93_Motion_Picture_Musical_or_Comedy "Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Motion Picture Musical or Comedy") for Dujardin and [Best Musical Score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Musical_Score "Golden Globe Award for Best Musical Score") for Bource.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Golden_Globes_2012_Winners-65)

At the [84th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/84th_Academy_Awards "84th Academy Awards"), _The Artist_ received ten nominations, winning five awards, including [Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture"), [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director") for Hazanavicius, [Best Actor in a Leading Role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor "Academy Award for Best Actor") for [Jean Dujardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Dujardin "Jean Dujardin"), [Best Costume Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Costume_Design "Academy Award for Best Costume Design"), and [Best Original Score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Score "Academy Award for Best Original Score").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Oscar_winners_2012-66)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Academy_Awards_2012_winners-67)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-68)

_**The Artist**_ is a 2011 French-Belgian[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-the_artist_2011-2)[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-9)[comedy-drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy-drama "Comedy-drama") film[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-11) in the style of a [black-and-white](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black-and-white "Black-and-white")[silent film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film") or [part-talkie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Part-talkie "Part-talkie").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-ACEFilmEditors-12)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-RottenTomatoes-14)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-15) It was written and directed by [Michel Hazanavicius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Hazanavicius "Michel Hazanavicius"), produced by [Thomas Langmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Langmann "Thomas Langmann") and stars [Jean Dujardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Dujardin "Jean Dujardin") and [Bérénice Bejo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo "Bérénice Bejo").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-16) The story takes place in [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los Angeles"), between 1927 and 1932, and focuses on the relationship between a rising young actress and an older silent film star as silent cinema falls out of fashion and is replaced by the "[talkies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_film "Sound film")".

_The Artist_ received widespread critical acclaim and won many accolades. Dujardin won [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival_Award_for_Best_Actor "Cannes Film Festival Award for Best Actor") at the [2011 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Cannes_Film_Festival "2011 Cannes Film Festival"), where the film premiered. The film was nominated for six [Golden Globes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award "Golden Globe Award"), the most of any 2011 film, and won three: [Best Motion Picture– Musical or Comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Motion_Picture_%E2%80%93_Musical_or_Comedy "Golden Globe Award for Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy"), [Best Original Score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Original_Score "Golden Globe Award for Best Original Score"), and [Best Actor– Motion Picture Musical or Comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Actor_%E2%80%93_Motion_Picture_Musical_or_Comedy "Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Motion Picture Musical or Comedy") for Dujardin. In January 2012, it was nominated for twelve [BAFTAs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA "BAFTA"), the most of any film from 2011,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-BBCBAFTA-17) and won seven, including [Best Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Film "BAFTA Award for Best Film"), [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Direction "BAFTA Award for Best Direction"), [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Actor_in_a_Leading_Role "BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role") for Dujardin, and [Best Original Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay "BAFTA Award for Best Original Screenplay") for Hazanavicius.

It was nominated for ten [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") and won five,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-BBCOscar-18) including [Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture"), [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director") for Hazanavicius, and [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor "Academy Award for Best Actor") for Dujardin, making him the first French actor ever to win in this category. It was also the first non-American/non-British film to ever win Best Picture,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-19) the first mainly silent film to win since 1927's _[Wings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wings\_(1927\_film) "Wings (1927 film)")_ won at the [1st Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Academy_Awards "1st Academy Awards") in 1929, the first film presented in the [4:3 aspect ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspect_ratio "Aspect ratio") to win since 1953's _[From Here to Eternity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/From\_Here\_to\_Eternity "From Here to Eternity")_, the first [black-and-white film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black-and-white_movie "Black-and-white movie") to win since 1993's _[Schindler's List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schindler's\_List "Schindler's List")_, though the latter contained limited colour sequences; and the first 100% black-and-white film to win since 1960's _[The Apartment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Apartment "The Apartment")_.

In France it was nominated for ten [César Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar_Awards "César Awards"),[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-BBCCesar-20) winning six, including [Best Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar_Award_for_Best_Film "César Award for Best Film"), [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar_Award_for_Best_Director "César Award for Best Director") for Hazanavicius, and [Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar_Award_for_Best_Actress "César Award for Best Actress") for Bejo. _The Artist_ has received more awards than any other French film.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-21)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

In 1927, [silent film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film") star George Valentin is posing for pictures outside the [premiere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiere "Premiere") of his latest hit film when a young woman, Peppy Miller, accidentally bumps into him. Valentin reacts with humor and shows off with Peppy for the cameras. The next day, Peppy is on the front page of _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ with the headline "Who's That Girl?" She capitalizes by auditioning as a dancer and is spotted by Valentin, who insists that she have a part in Kinograph Studios' next production, despite objections from studio boss Al Zimmer. While performing a scene in which they dance together, Valentin and Peppy show great chemistry. With a little guidance from Valentin, who draws a [beauty spot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_spot "Beauty spot") on her cheek, Peppy rises through the industry, earning more prominent starring roles.

Two years later, Zimmer announces plans to cease production of silent films at Kinograph Studios, but Valentin is dismissive, insisting that sound is just a fad. In a dream, he begins hearing sounds from his environment (as does the audience) but cannot speak himself. He decides to leave the studio for the chance to produce, finance, and direct his own silent film, _Tears of Love_. The film opens on the same day as Peppy's new sound film _Beauty Spot_ and the [1929 stock market crash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_crash_of_1929 "Wall Street crash of 1929"). Valentin's only chance of avoiding bankruptcy is for his film to be a hit. Unfortunately, audiences flock to Peppy's film instead, while only a few people attend Valentin's. With Valentin ruined, his wife, Doris, kicks him out, and he moves into an apartment with his valet/chauffeur, Clifton, and his dog. Peppy quickly becomes the first of several major new Hollywood sound film stars.

Later, the bankrupt Valentin is forced to auction his personal effects, and after realizing he has not paid the loyal Clifton in over a year, gives him his car before firing him. Depressed and drunk, Valentin sets fire to a stack of his old films. As the [nitrate film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrocellulose#Film "Nitrocellulose") blazes out of control, he is overwhelmed by the smoke and passes out inside the burning house, clutching a single film canister. However, Valentin's dog attracts the help of a nearby policeman, and after being rescued, Valentin is hospitalized for injuries suffered in the fire. Peppy visits the hospital and discovers that the film he rescued is the one with them dancing together. She asks for him to be moved to her house to recuperate. Valentin awakens in a bed at her house to find that Clifton is now working for Peppy. His ego hurt, Valentin shows ingratitude for Peppy having taken him in, prompting Clifton to remind him of his changing luck.

Peppy insists to Zimmer that Valentin co-star in her next film, threatening to quit Kinograph if he does not agree. After Valentin learns that Peppy bought his possessions at auction, he returns in despair to his burnt-out apartment. Peppy arrives and finds that Valentin is about to attempt suicide. She tells him she only wanted to help him. They embrace, and Valentin tells her it is no use; no one wants to hear him speak. Remembering Valentin's superb dancing ability, Peppy persuades Zimmer to let her make a [musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_film#The_classical_sound_era "Musical film") production so Valentin can avoid the humiliation of having to speak.

Now the audience hears sound for the second time, as the film starts rolling for a dance scene with Peppy and Valentin and their tap-dancing can be heard. Once the choreography is complete, the two dancers are heard panting. The director of the musical calls, "Cut!" to which Zimmer adds: "Perfect. Beautiful. Could you give me just one more?" Valentin, in his only audible line, replies "With pleasure," revealing a [French accent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_accent "French accent").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-themarysue-22) The camera then pulls back to the sounds of the film crew as they prepare to shoot another take.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")]

### Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/%C3%89quipe_The_Artist_Cannes_2011.jpg/500px-%C3%89quipe_The_Artist_Cannes_2011.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%C3%89quipe_The_Artist_Cannes_2011.jpg)

Some of the cast and crew at the [2011 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Cannes_Film_Festival "2011 Cannes Film Festival"): (left to right), score composer [Ludovic Bource](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludovic_Bource "Ludovic Bource"), director [Michel Hazanavicius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Hazanavicius "Michel Hazanavicius"), stars [Missi Pyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missi_Pyle "Missi Pyle"), [Bérénice Bejo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo "Bérénice Bejo"), and [Jean Dujardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Dujardin "Jean Dujardin"), director of photography [Guillaume Schiffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_Schiffman "Guillaume Schiffman") and producer [Thomas Langmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Langmann "Thomas Langmann").

Director [Michel Hazanavicius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Hazanavicius "Michel Hazanavicius") had been fantasizing about making a [silent film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film") for many years, both because many filmmakers he admires emerged in the silent era, and because of the image-driven nature of the form. According to Hazanavicius, his wish to make a silent film was at first not taken seriously, but after the financial success of his spy-film pastiches _[OSS 117: Cairo, Nest of Spies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OSS\_117:\_Cairo,\_Nest\_of\_Spies "OSS 117: Cairo, Nest of Spies")_ and _[OSS 117: Lost in Rio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OSS\_117:\_Lost\_in\_Rio "OSS 117: Lost in Rio")_, producers started to express interest. The forming of the film's narrative started with Hazanavicius' desire to work again with actors [Jean Dujardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Dujardin "Jean Dujardin") and [Bérénice Bejo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo "Bérénice Bejo"), who had both starred in _OSS 117: Cairo, Nest of Spies_. Hazanavicius chose the form of a [melodrama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melodrama_(film_genre) "Melodrama (film genre)"), mostly because he thought many of the films from the silent era that have aged best are of that genre. He did extensive research about 1920s Hollywood, and studied silent films to find the right techniques to make the story comprehensible without having to use too many [intertitles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertitle "Intertitle"). The screenplay took four months to write and was principally inspired by the 1928 silent comedy, _[Show People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Show\_People "Show People")_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-presskitmh-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-24)

Chief among the influences shaping the screenplay's protagonist was [Douglas Fairbanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Fairbanks "Douglas Fairbanks"). The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences' recent book _Douglas Fairbanks_, by [Jeffrey Vance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Vance "Jeffrey Vance"), as well as the academy's Douglas Fairbanks exhibition and screening events both in Los Angeles and New York City, afforded Hollywood's first swashbuckling hero and the academy's first president some significant media attention.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-25)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-26)

### Filming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Filming")]

[Principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") on _The Artist_ began in November 2010,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-27) taking place over the course of thirty-five days,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-BAFTARed-28) made in the 1.33:1 screen ratio commonly used in the silent film era. Though presented in black-and-white, it was shot in color by [cinematographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinematographer "Cinematographer")[Guillaume Schiffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_Schiffman "Guillaume Schiffman").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-time-29) All the technical details, including lenses, lighting and camera moves, were calibrated to aesthetically match silent films of the period.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-30) To recreate the slightly sped-up look of 1920s silent films, the film was shot at a slightly lower [frame rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frame_rate "Frame rate") of 22 fps as opposed to the standard 24 fps.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-31) Most of the film is silent, except for two brief scenes with sound as well as the [non-diegetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinematic_techniques#Sound "Cinematic techniques") soundtrack. Throughout the shoot, Hazanavicius played music from classic Hollywood films while the actors performed.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-presskitmh-23)

The film was produced by La Petite Reine and ARP Sélection for 13.47 million euro, including co-production support from [Studio 37](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_37 "Studio 37") and [France 3 Cinéma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_3_Cin%C3%A9ma "France 3 Cinéma"), and pre-sales investment from [StudioCanal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/StudioCanal "StudioCanal") and CinéCinéma.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-outofcomp-32) The cast and the crew included both French and American members.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-presskitmh-23) All the scenes were shot in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), primarily in [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los Angeles"), but also in downtown theaters, restaurants and houses, including the one in which [Mary Pickford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Pickford "Mary Pickford") lived. Soundstage work was done at [Red Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren-Mar_Studios "Ren-Mar Studios"), and the studio lot itself doubled for part of the fictional Kinograph Studios lot, with Red's Lillian Way entrance doubling as the Kinograph entrance in several sequences. The iconic [Bradbury Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradbury_Building "Bradbury Building") in downtown L.A. provided the location for the film's distinctive staircase sequence. The dance sequence that closes the film took seventeen takes, and required Dujardin and Bejo to spend five months studying tap dancing, with Dujardin claiming that "in the first week it's fun, the fifth week it's a little boring, at the end it's thrilling".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-33)

American [costume designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costume_design "Costume design")[Mark Bridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Bridges_(costume_designer) "Mark Bridges (costume designer)") created the wardrobe for the film's cast.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-sfgate-34)

### Music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Music")]

Main article: [_The Artist_ (soundtrack)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(soundtrack) "The Artist (soundtrack)")

The [film's music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_score "Film score") was largely composed by [Ludovic Bource](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludovic_Bource "Ludovic Bource"), but includes works by other composers such as [Alberto Ginastera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Ginastera "Alberto Ginastera")'s "Estancia". The soundtrack was recorded in Belgium by the [Brussels Philharmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels_Philharmonic "Brussels Philharmonic") and was conducted by Ernst Van Tiel; the Brussels Jazz Orchestra also cooperated. The recording took place during six days in April 2011 at [Flagey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_Flagey "Place Flagey")'s Studio 4 in Brussels.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-35)

The film's climactic scene is set to [Bernard Herrmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Herrmann "Bernard Herrmann")'s "Scène d'amour" from [his score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertigo_(film_score) "Vertigo (film score)") to [Alfred Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock "Alfred Hitchcock")'s film _[Vertigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertigo\_(film) "Vertigo (film)")_. In _Vertigo_, that composition similarly accompanies an extended scene without dialogue. Only one song (sung, with lyrics) is used in the soundtrack, "[Pennies from Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennies_from_Heaven_(song) "Pennies from Heaven (song)")", sung by [Rose "Chi-Chi" Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_Murphy "Rose Murphy") (uncredited). This song was written in 1936 although the film is set between 1927 and 1932. The soundtrack was released on 10 October in France, and 21 October in the U.K. and U.S. through [Sony Classical Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Classical_Records "Sony Classical Records").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-36)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Box office

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Box office")]

_The Artist_ grossed $44,671,682 in North America, along with $88,761,174 in other territories for a worldwide total of $133,432,856.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Boxofficemojo-3) After its success at the Academy Awards, the film saw a moderate boost the following week on the box office in North America. It appeared on the week's top 10 chart and got an increase of 34% while expanding its release from 966 theaters to 1,756.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-47)

### Critical response

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Critical response")]

On review aggregator [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes") the film has an approval rating of 95% based on 327 reviews, with an average rating of 8.8/10. The website's critical consensus states, "A crowd-pleasing tribute to the magic of silent cinema, _The Artist_ is a clever, joyous film with delightful performances and visual style to spare."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-RottenTomatoes-14) At [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which assigns a [weighted average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_average "Weighted average") rating to reviews, the film received an average score of 89 out of 100, based on 41 critics, indicating "universal acclaim".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Metacritic-48) Audiences surveyed by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film an average grade of "A" on an A+ to F scale.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-49)

Mark Adams of _[Screen Daily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen\_International "Screen International")_ called the film "a real pleasure"; "propelled elegantly forward by delightful performances from Jean Dujardin and Bérénice Bejo it is the most unlikely of feel-good movies." He added however: "The film does feel a little sluggish towards the end of the first third as the music is a little repetitive and the intertitles are infrequent, but Hazanavicius manages to give the film a real sense of charm and warmth, and film fans will be competing to spot visual and musical references."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-50) Peter Bradshaw of _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ described how the film "had me on my feet cheering throughout the final credits" and stated "I can't wait to see it again".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-51)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Jean_Dujardin_2014.jpg/250px-Jean_Dujardin_2014.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jean_Dujardin_2014.jpg)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo_2014_2.jpg/250px-B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo_2014_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo_2014_2.jpg)

The performances of [Jean Dujardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Dujardin "Jean Dujardin") and [Bérénice Bejo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9r%C3%A9nice_Bejo "Bérénice Bejo") garnered critical acclaim, earning them [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") nominations for [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor "Academy Award for Best Actor") and [Best Supporting Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress") respectively, with Dujardin winning his category.

Geoffrey McNab at _[The Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Independent "The Independent")_ called the film "both a surefire crowdpleaser and a magnificent piece of film-making" in his 5 star review from the [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-52) Rick Groen of _[The Globe and Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Globe\_and\_Mail "The Globe and Mail")_ assessed _The Artist_ highly, noting the film "uses old technology to dazzling effect to illustrate the insistent conquest of a new technology."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-53) Sukanya Verma for [Rediff.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rediff.com "Rediff.com") feels _The Artist_ is an extremely well-researched film and is an instant classic.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Review_:_The_Artist-54) David Thomson of _[The New Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Republic "The New Republic")_ called _The Artist_ an "accomplished and witty entertainment" and went on to write, "Whether Hazanavicius can do more things as elegant and touching, without the gimmick of silence, remains to be seen (and heard). Meanwhile, he is to be congratulated on the grounds of pleasure alone. He may be due for much more in the way of rewards."[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-55)_[Chicago Sun-Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago\_Sun-Times "Chicago Sun-Times")_[film critic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_criticism "Film criticism")[Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") gave the film four out of four stars, praising the performances, and calling the film "one of the most entertaining films in many a moon, a film that charms because of its story, its performances and because of the sly way it plays with being silent and black and white."[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-56)

Writing for _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant\_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_, Jaime N. Christley gave the film one-and-a-half out of four stars, explaining Michel Hazanavicius ignores "everything that's fascinating and memorable about the era, focusing instead on a patchwork of general knowledge, so eroded of inconvenient facts that it doesn't even qualify as a _roman à clef_."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-57)_[America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America\_(magazine) "America (magazine)")_ argued that while Jean Dujardin carried the film, Bejo's performance was disappointing.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-america-58)

### Kim Novak controversy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Kim Novak controversy")]

On 9 January 2012, actress [Kim Novak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Novak "Kim Novak") stated that "rape" had been metaphorically committed in the film's licensed use of a portion of [Bernard Herrmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Herrmann "Bernard Herrmann")'s score from [Alfred Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock "Alfred Hitchcock")'s 1958 film _[Vertigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertigo\_(film) "Vertigo (film)")_ (in which Novak starred). The final portion of _The Artist_ is accompanied not by original music, but by a 1992 recording of the Herrmann composition _Scene d'Amour_, conducted by [Elmer Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elmer_Bernstein "Elmer Bernstein"). In the article published, by _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_, she stated that "I feel as if my body—or at least my body of work—has been violated by the movie."[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Vertigo-59) "This film should've been able to stand on its own without depending on Bernard Herrmann's score from Alfred Hitchcock's _Vertigo_ to provide more drama" and that "It is morally wrong for the artistry of our industry to use and abuse famous pieces of work to gain attention and applause for other than what they were intended", ending her comments with "Shame on them!"[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-CNN-60)

In response, director Hazanavicius released a statement:

> _The Artist_ was made as a love letter to cinema, and grew out of my (and all of my cast and crew's) admiration and respect for movies throughout history. It was inspired by the work of Hitchcock, [Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Lang "Fritz Lang"), [Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ford "John Ford"), [Lubitsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Lubitsch "Ernst Lubitsch"), [Murnau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._W._Murnau "F. W. Murnau") and [Wilder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Wilder "Billy Wilder"). I love Bernard Herrmann and his music has been used in many different films and I'm very pleased to have it in mine. I respect Kim Novak greatly and I'm sorry to hear she disagrees.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-61)

Hazanavicius also told [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN") "I used music from another movie, but it's not illegal. We paid for that, we asked for that and we had the permission to do it. For me there is no real controversy.... I feel sorry for her, but there's a lot of movies with music from other movies, directors do that all the time and I'm not sure it's a big deal."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-CNN-60)

In May 2011, when the film was first shown at the Cannes Festival, [Todd McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todd_McCarthy "Todd McCarthy") from _[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hollywood\_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")_ mentioned the use of Herrmann's music, "Hazanavicius and Bource daringly choose to explicitly employ Bernard Herrmann's love theme from _Vertigo_, which is dramatically effective in its own right but is so well known that it yanks you out of one film and places you in the mind-set of another. Surely some sort of reworked equivalent would have been a better idea."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-McCarthy-62)

### Accolades

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Artist_(film)&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Accolades")]

Main article: [List of accolades received by _The Artist_ (film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_accolades_received_by_The_Artist_(film) "List of accolades received by The Artist (film)")

At the [65th British Academy Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_British_Academy_Film_Awards "65th British Academy Film Awards"), the film won seven awards, including Best Film, Best Actor for Dujardin, Best Original Screenplay for Hazanavicius, Cinematography for Schiffman, Costume Design for Bridges and Original Score for [Ludovic Bource](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludovic_Bource "Ludovic Bource").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Orange_BAFTA_Film_Award_Winners-63)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-BAFTA_2012_Winners-64) At the [69th Golden Globe Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/69th_Golden_Globe_Awards "69th Golden Globe Awards"), the film was nominated for six [Golden Globes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globes "Golden Globes") to win three of them; [Best Motion Picture– Musical or Comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Motion_Picture_%E2%80%93_Musical_or_Comedy "Golden Globe Award for Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy"), [Best Actor– Motion Picture Musical or Comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Actor_%E2%80%93_Motion_Picture_Musical_or_Comedy "Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Motion Picture Musical or Comedy") for Dujardin and [Best Musical Score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Musical_Score "Golden Globe Award for Best Musical Score") for Bource.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Golden_Globes_2012_Winners-65)

At the [84th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/84th_Academy_Awards "84th Academy Awards"), _The Artist_ received ten nominations, winning five awards, including [Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture"), [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director") for Hazanavicius, [Best Actor in a Leading Role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor "Academy Award for Best Actor") for [Jean Dujardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Dujardin "Jean Dujardin"), [Best Costume Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Costume_Design "Academy Award for Best Costume Design"), and [Best Original Score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Score "Academy Award for Best Original Score").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Oscar_winners_2012-66)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-Academy_Awards_2012_winners-67)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Artist_(film)#cite_note-68)
